newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU puts forward plan to protect financial services consumers.
newsitem.headline: EU puts forward plan to protect financial services consumers.

text.p: The European Commission announced on Thursday it was planning a raft of new legislation to improve consumer protection in the financial services sector, while adopting a wait-and-see approach on some issues.

"We must not only enhance consumer confidence in the single market for financial services but also ensure a level playing field for cross-border service providers," the EU single market commissioner Mario Monti said in a statement.

The Commission said that following publication of a green paper on the issue last year, consultations had revealed the need for action in several key areas, and not least the ever-growing area of distance contracts for financial services.
The Commission plans to submit a proposal for a binding directive on this by the autumn.

"The proposed directive will help to raise consumer confidence whilst enabling service providers to market their services across the EU without unnecessary obstacles," the Commission said in a statement.

It said it would also decide by the beginning of next year whether to propose binding legislation to regulate financial intermediaries and will propose to review existing legislation on insurance intermediaries early next year.

It also plans by mid-1998 to review its 1987 directive on consumer credit and to carry out pilot projects on over- indebtedness, some aimed at improving consumer information and education, the Commission said.
The Commission said it would propose by the autumn a directive aimed at ensuring insurance coverage for victims of car accidents which happen abroad.
"This will provide that accident victims can lodge a claim against an insurer anywhere in the EU and that claims representatives will be nominated," it said.

The Commission said it was deferring decisions on whether to make proposals for binding action on mortgage credit until the beginning of next year and holding off on binding legislation on new means of payment, notably electronic payment, in the hope that EU members would follow non-binding recommendations.
